Lead isotope provenance functions

Source: vignettes/Pb_Iso_prov.Rmd
Pb_Iso_prov.Rmd

Introduction

Provenance studies using lead isotope analysis use three ratios of the four naturally occurring lead isotopes. These are: 206Pb/204Pb, 207Pb/204Pb, 208Pb/204Pb.

The isotopic compositions in LIA are initially represented in a three dimensional coordinate system (Albarede, Davis, Gentelli, et al. 2024).

However, current approaches to lead isotope analysis, such as amalia(), rely heavily on visual inspection or simple distance-based metrics, methods that struggle to capture the complex structure and overlaps within large isotopic datasets. As a result, provenance interpretations often differ substantially between researchers, even when studying the same assemblages. By contrast, an algorithmic framework provides a systematic, data-driven alternative that detects patterns, reduces overlaps, and minimizes subjective interpretation. This shift not only improves reproducibility but also opens the door to identifying previously unrecognised ore sources (Shnyr et al. 2026).

The lead isotope provenance functions follow the ASTR schema and only accept ASTR objects. Working with ASTR objects is described here

For the purposes of demonstration, lead isotope data from the Tel Dor silver hoards will be used as sample data (Shnyr et al. 2026), and a modified GlobaLID database, containing lead isotope ratios grouped by the Political province/region variable, will be used as reference data.

Provenance functions

There are two main methods which can be used for provenance analysis. The first is the standard Euclidean distance function, with an added mass fractionation correction (Albarede, Davis, Gentelli, et al. 2024), and the second is a machine learning method, where a pre-trained extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) model is used to obtain provenance probabilities (Shnyr et al. 2026). In both cases, sample and reference data are provided as ASTR objects.

Creating reference data object

Before using the functions, the reference data must be transformed into an ASTR_Pbiso_ref_data object. This can be achieved using the as_pbiso_ref_data() function, which removes all variables except the ASTR_context designated as the grouping variable and the lead isotope ratios. The reference dataset can sometimes contain groups with too few samples for reliable analysis. It is therefore advisable to exclude these groups from the reference dataset. The min_groupsize argument can be used to set an integer cutoff value. Only groups containing at least min_groupsize samples will be retained.

GlobalLID_ASTR_ref <- as_pbiso_ref_data(GlobaLID_ASTR, group = "Political province/region", min_groupsize = 5L)

Standard Euclidean distance

The standard model for estimating three dimensional distances for lead isotope values involves measuring the Euclidean distance between two vectors, x→\vec{x} and x′→\vec{x'}. This calculation follows the established formula:

d(x→,x′→)=∑i=1n(xi−xi′)2d(\vec{x}, \vec{x'}) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - x'_i)^2}

This is the method used by the function pb_iso_prov_dist() when the dist_type value is set to "ed", which stands for ‘Euclidean distance’.

According to Albarede, Davis, Blichert-Toft, et al. (2024), the standard method fails to account for statistical errors. These errors are addressed by weighting the data with the full covariance matrix WW of the NIST 981 lead isotope reference material. The adjusted distance is calculated as:

d=(x−x′)TW−1(x−x′)d = \sqrt{(x - x')^T W^{-1} (x - x')}.

In this formula, TT denotes the transpose of the vector.

euc_dist(tel_dor, GlobalLID_ASTR_ref, n = 1)

Algorithm accounting for mass dependent fractionation

Recently, Albarede, Davis, Gentelli, et al. (2024) introduced a Pb isotope provenance algorithm that significantly improves the correction of mass-dependent fractionation, a long standing challenge in lead isotope analysis.

The methodology utilizes the distance did_i between an artefact and the mass-dependent fractionation line passing through ore ii. This is implemented by setting dist_type to "mfd". Provided that lead isotope ratios differ by less than one decimal point, the respective fractionation lines are considered parallel.

The distance did_i is computed using the vector ΔXi→=(x→i−x→0)\vec{\Delta X_i} = (\vec{x}_i - \vec{x}_0), where x→0\vec{x}_0 represents the artefact and x→i\vec{x}_i represents the ore.The artefact is represented as:

x→0=[(206Pb/204Pb)0,(207Pb/204Pb)0,(208Pb/204Pb)0]\vec{x}_0=\left[\left(^{206}Pb/^{204}Pb\right)_0,\left(^{207}Pb/^{204}Pb\right)_0,\left(^{208}Pb/^{204}Pb\right)_0\right]

The ore is represented as:

x→i=[(206Pb/204Pb)i,(207Pb/204Pb)i,(208Pb/204Pb)i]\vec{x}_i=\left[\left(^{206}Pb/^{204}Pb\right)_i,\left(^{207}Pb/^{204}Pb\right)_i,\left(^{208}Pb/^{204}Pb\right)_i\right]

The mass-dependent fractionation line is defined by the vector v→\vec{v}:

v→=[2(206Pb/204Pb)0,3(207Pb/204Pb)0,4(208Pb/204Pb)0]\vec{v}=\left[2\left(^{206}Pb/^{204}Pb\right)_0,3\left(^{207}Pb/^{204}Pb\right)_0,4\left(^{208}Pb/^{204}Pb\right)_0\right]

The digits in v→\vec{v} correspond to the atomic mass differences of the isotopes. With n→=v→/||v→||\vec{n} = \vec{v}/||\vec{v}|| as the unit vector, the distance did_i is calculated using the cross-product:

di=||ΔXi→×n→||d_i = ||\vec{\Delta X_i} \times \vec{n}||

The fractionation factor fif_i is computed as a dot product:

fi=ΔXi→⋅n→f_i = \vec{\Delta X_i} \cdot \vec{n}

To obtain a dimensionless distance, the error matrix WW is defined as:

W=[2xx*0003xy*0004xz*][10.960.940.9610.960.940.961][2xx*0003xy*0004xz*]W= \begin{bmatrix} 2x^*_x & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 3x^*_y & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 4x^*_z\\ \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.96 & 0.94\\ 0.96 & 1 & 0.96\\ 0.94 & 0.96 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2x^*_x & 0 & 0\\ 0 & 3x^*_y & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 4x^*_z\\ \end{bmatrix}

The outer matrices are diagonal standard deviation matrices for common lead, with a fractionation factor ss of 0.001. Squared distances d2d^2 are normalised to the two dimensional shadow of WW perpendicular to n→\vec{n}. This requires Gram Schmidt orthogonalisation to find perpendicular vectors. Since WW is derived from reference materials, this metric is not a formal Mahalanobis distance. Normalised squared distances follow a chi squared distribution with two degrees of freedom. Consequently, ores with d2d^2 values exceeding 5.99 are rejected at the 95% confidence level.

mf_dist(tel_dor, GlobalLID_ASTR_ref, n = 1, s = 0.001)

The pb_iso_prov_dist() provides a wrapper for them and allows to calculate all age models simultaneously. All distance functions use the as_pbiso_ref_data() function, regular ASTR objects to lead isotope reference data.

pb_iso_prov_dist(tel_dor, GlobaLID_ASTR, ref_group = "Political province/region",
                 dist_type = "all")

Machine learning model

Models trained using pb_iso_train_data() go through a data processing pipeline as outlined by (Shnyr et al. 2026):

  • Outlier identification
  • SMOTE data imputation
  • XGBoost Classification and model training.

Outlier identification

Outlier identification and elimination are achieved using the DBSCAN (Density Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise) algorithm, which can identify outliers and subgroup patterns within regions.

DBSCAN facilitates the removal of outliers and the formation of clusters within lead isotopic data, reducing potential overlaps between regions.

The neighbourhood radius (ϵ\epsilon) determines the appropriate value for clustering. This is controlled by the .eps argument.

To ensure reliability, only samples above a certain number should be clustered. This is controlled by the .minSize argument.

SMOTE data imputation

SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over sampling Technique) is a methodology that creates synthetic data points for the minority class through interpolation.

Using SMOTE enables ML models to better identify patterns in the data, potentially leading to more accurate predictions.

The k neighbour parameter in the SMOTE algorithm controls how many nearby data points are considered when generating synthetic samples for minority classes. A smaller k neighbour value focuses on closer neighbours, while a larger value includes a broader range of neighbours, affecting the diversity of synthetic samples (Chawla et al. 2002).

XGBoost classification and model training

The XGBoost algorithm was applied to train a binary classification model using the three isotopic ratios as input features and the resulting regional cluster names, previously derived from DBSCAN, as target labels.

This iterative process involved encoding the data, applying SMOTE, and training the XGBoost model for each cluster. The final model is a list of individual XGBoost models that can effectively distinguish between target and non target classes, leveraging the refined dataset for reliable predictions.

ml_model <- pb_iso_train_data(GlobalLID_ASTR_ref)

Machine learning based provenance prediction

Providing the sample data ASTR object with the model created usingpb_iso_train_data() produces a new ASTR object containing the provenance probabilities for the given reference data groups.

pb_iso_prov_predict(tel_dor, model_list = ml_model, .top = 1)

Albarede, Francis, Gillan Davis, Liesel Gentelli, et al. 2024. “Bullion Mixtures in Silver Coinage from Ancient Greece and Egypt.” Journal of Archaeological Science 162 (February): 105918. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105918.
Chawla, N. V., K. W. Bowyer, L. O. Hall, and W. P. Kegelmeyer. 2002. “SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique.” Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 16 (June): 321–57. https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.953.
Shnyr, Evgeny, Tsvi Kuflik, Karan Desai, and Tzilla Eshel. 2026. “Determining the Origins of Phoenician Silver: Exploring the Potential of Machine Learning for Lead Isotope Analysis.” Journal of Archaeological Science 188 (April): 106–499. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2026.106499.
